centralQuestion: How did one injured engineer survive both1945 atomic bombings, and what does official double recognition mean?
thesis: One injured shipbuilding engineer returned from Hiroshima to his home city, Nagasaki, before the second bombing. His official double-exposure recognition does not make him the only double survivor. His later witness serves remembrance and nuclear abolition.
viewerPayoff: One injured shipbuilding engineer returned from Hiroshima to his home city, Nagasaki, before the second bombing. His official double-exposure recognition does not make him the only double survivor. His later witness serves remembrance and nuclear abolition.

visualOpportunities.title: One man, two cities
visualOpportunities.description: Intimate young engineer portrait; true story identification and explicit reconstruction disclosure. Move from face toward ship-design papers and1945 setting; same engineer identity. Hiroshima morning context; date and restrained distant light, no mushroom-cloud spectacle. Ash and damaged environment; bandaged same engineer, no graphic wounds. Hiroshima to Nagasaki geographic map animated as city link, then rail travel; no claimed exact itinerary. Nagasaki August9; same bandaged man at design office, no invented dialogue enacted. Office light intensifies and papers move, aftermath held; second event unmistakably separated by city/date. Reflective aftermath; wife/infant survival stated without invented family reunion scene. City absence and ruins acknowledge lives lost; no triumph or graphic victims. Geographic two-city record resolves official double-exposure distinction, no fabricated certificate. Plural survivor distinction clear in caption; map retains two cities. Life dates1916–2010 and93; no unverified aged likeness or false archival portrait. Quiet empty drafting desk/paper toward soft daylight, later witness and abolition message; no unrelated slogan.
